opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is honestly one of the hardest parts of post-training, and I think it's underrated. When you're training a model, you're never training on one dataset in isolation. You have dozens of data sources, some for reasoning, some for creative writing, some for safety and refusals, some for tool use, and they all pull on the model in different directions. A lot of the weird behaviors you see come not from one bad dataset but from the interaction between two that each look perfectly fine on their own.

A classic example is refusals. You add data teaching the model to decline genuinely harmful requests, and suddenly it gets more cautious in totally unrelated places. It starts hedging on creative writing or refusing a benign medical question. Nothing in either dataset was wrong; the model just generalized a pattern more broadly than you intended. Or you push hard on concise answers for one use case and it bleeds into domains where people actually want depth.

So on detection, a few things matter. First, really broad evals, and not just the headline benchmarks. You want evals that capture behaviors and personality: over-refusal, verbosity, sycophancy, how it handles ambiguity. Many of these regressions are invisible if you only track accuracy on math and code.

Second, ablations. When you see a regression, you ask which data mixture introduced it. You train smaller runs adding or removing specific datasets and see which combination triggers the behavior. It's expensive, but it's the most reliable way to isolate causality instead of guessing.

Third, and I think people underestimate this, just talking to the model a lot. Qualitative vibe-checking catches things evals miss. You notice that the model got a little preachy, or it's suddenly overusing a certain phrase, and that's often the first signal that two data sources are fighting.

On fixing, it's usually some mix of rebalancing the data mixture, writing targeted contrastive data that teaches the model where the boundary actually is, like "refuse this, but help with this very similar-looking thing," and sometimes rethinking the underlying spec. Often the conflict exists because we weren't clear about what we wanted the model to do in the first place. The data reflects ambiguity in the behavior spec, and the model faithfully learns that ambiguity.

I think long-term this becomes more of a science. Right now it's still a lot of craft and intuition, but there's huge room for better tooling around attributing behaviors back to data and predicting interactions before you spend the compute on a full run.

r001.rationale: The response describes failure behaviors in a model trained on interacting data sources, but does not say that different trained models have distinct characteristic failure modes.

r002.rationale: It describes unintended side effects from conflicting data sources and gives ways to address them, including rebalancing the mixture and adding targeted contrastive data.

r003.rationale: It recommends evaluations, ablations, and qualitative checks for debugging, but does not identify software engineering techniques as useful.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that data interactions are one of the hardest things to reason about in training, because almost nothing is additive. You add a new dataset to improve, say, coding, and you think of it as a local change, but it's not local. It shifts the distribution the model sees, it changes what gets reinforced, and suddenly your model is a bit more terse in conversation, or it's more sycophantic, or it stops refusing things it used to refuse. And none of that was in the dataset you added. It emerged from how the new data interacted with everything else.

So the first thing I'd say is you have to stop thinking in terms of "does this dataset work" and start thinking in terms of "what does this dataset do to the mixture." Which means you need evals that are much broader than the capability you're targeting. Every time I've seen a regression that surprised people, it was because they had great evals for the thing they were trying to improve and basically nothing for the thing they accidentally broke. So a lot of the work is just building a wide enough net of behavioral evals — tone, instruction following, refusals, calibration, verbosity, all of it — that you'd actually notice a side effect.

The second thing is being very systematic about ablations. It's tempting to change five things at once because training runs are expensive, but then when something goes wrong you have no idea what caused it. I'd much rather run smaller-scale experiments where you vary one component of the mixture at a time and build an intuition for what each piece is doing. It's slower, but you accumulate real knowledge about your data instead of just a pile of checkpoints.

And then on the fixing side, I've become pretty skeptical of patching. The instinct when you see a bad behavior is to go generate a bunch of examples of the good behavior and throw them in. Sometimes that works, but often it just creates a new interaction — now the model has learned a surface heuristic for when to behave a certain way, and that heuristic misfires somewhere else. So I try to ask, what is the model actually learning from this data, as a generalization, not as a set of examples? And often the better fix is to remove or rewrite something upstream rather than add a counterweight. Subtracting data is underrated.

The last piece is actually looking at the outputs. Not just the aggregate numbers. Reading transcripts, reading a lot of them, from different stages of training. A huge number of data interaction problems are visible qualitatively way before they show up in a metric, because the metric was never designed to catch them. The people who are good at this tend to be the ones who have this almost obsessive habit of reading model outputs and noticing when something feels slightly off, and then going and tracing that back to the data. I don't think there's a shortcut around that.

r001.rationale: The response describes behaviors that can emerge after adding data, but it does not say that different trained models have distinct characteristic failure modes.

r002.rationale: It discusses unintended side effects and ways to detect or fix them, but does not address contradictory datasets or raise that specific prevention question.

r003.rationale: It recommends evals, ablations, and transcript review, but does not identify software engineering techniques as useful for debugging data interactions.

astra-6.text:
I think the hard part is that a dataset can look good in isolation, but when you mix it with other data, the effect can be quite different. So I’d start with the behavior: what got worse, and on which kinds of examples? An aggregate score can hide a lot of those regressions.

Then I’d form hypotheses and run controlled ablations—remove a source, change its weight, or vary the order in which the model sees it—to understand whether the issue comes from that source or from an interaction. You want to change one thing at a time where possible, because otherwise it’s hard to know what actually fixed the problem.

And the fix isn’t necessarily more data. It might be changing the mixture, resolving conflicting examples, or improving the quality of a small subset. The important thing is to test the fix against both the failure you identified and the capabilities you want to preserve. It’s an iterative loop of inspecting behavior, testing a hypothesis, and checking the tradeoffs.

r001.rationale: The response discusses regressions and tradeoffs in a model, but does not say that different trained models have distinct characteristic failure modes.

r002.rationale: It addresses conflicting examples and recommends testing fixes against the identified failure while checking capabilities to preserve, covering how to avoid unintended side effects from contradictory data.

r003.rationale: It recommends controlled ablations and hypothesis testing, but does not identify software engineering techniques as useful for debugging data-interaction problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the tricky part is that a dataset can look perfectly reasonable in isolation, and then, when you mix it with other data, you get behavior you didn’t anticipate. So I’d start with the behavior: what changed, and on which tasks? Did the model become better at following instructions but worse at recognizing when it should ask a clarifying question?

Then you need controlled experiments. Hold the evaluation fixed, change the mixture, remove a subset, or vary its weight, and see whether the effect persists. Looking at individual examples helps you form hypotheses, but an example alone doesn’t establish what caused the regression.

And the fix isn’t always removing bad data. Sometimes two useful sources are teaching conflicting behaviors, or one is overwhelming the other. You might need to rebalance them, make the intended context clearer, or change when they enter training. The important thing is to check that you’ve fixed the underlying behavior across different settings, rather than just improved the metric that first exposed it.

r001.rationale: The response describes behavior changes from mixing data in one model, but does not say that different trained models have distinct characteristic failure modes.

r002.rationale: It addresses conflicting behaviors from useful data sources and suggests rebalancing them, clarifying context, or changing when they enter training to prevent unwanted effects.

r003.rationale: It recommends controlled experiments, but does not identify software engineering techniques as useful for debugging data interaction problems.
